title: Infosys AI Services Could Be Nearly Half Its Work in 2-3 Years, CEO Salil Parekh Says
excerpt: AI services were over 8% of Infosys revenue last quarter and are growing at a double-digit rate sequentially, Parekh told the Bloomberg New Economy Forum. About 80,000 of its roughly 300,000 employees already use coding tools.
body:
• Infosys CEO Salil Parekh said AI services — over 8% of revenue last quarter and growing at a double-digit rate sequentially — could reach 20-30% of the company's work within a few quarters.
  • Extrapolating that pace, Parekh said AI could account for almost half of Infosys's work within two to three years.
  • The work includes building AI agents, coding, and modernising legacy client systems; about 80,000 of roughly 300,000 employees already use coding tools.
  • Infosys hired 20,000 fresh graduates last year and plans another 20,000 this financial year, training them in AI before deployment.

Infosys expects artificial intelligence services to become a far larger part of its business over the next few years, potentially accounting for nearly half of its work within two to three years, CEO and Managing Director Salil Parekh said at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026, according to PTI reporting carried by Storyboard18.

Parekh said AI services contributed more than 8% of Infosys's revenue in the previous quarter and were growing at a double-digit rate sequentially. The segment includes developing AI agents, coding solutions and upgrading legacy technology for clients.

"It (AI services) is growing at a fantastic pace. If you sort of extrapolate that by a few quarters, you already start to see that's 20-30% of our work in a few quarters, and maybe in two or three years, almost half of our work."

— Salil Parekh, CEO and MD, Infosys

An extrapolation, not a target

Parekh's framing matters: he presented the trajectory as an extrapolation of current growth, not a company target. Even so, the arithmetic is striking. A business that is roughly one-twelfth of revenue today would, on his numbers, be one-fifth to nearly one-third of all work within a few quarters — a pace that implies AI services are not just winning new contracts but absorbing work that would previously have been billed as conventional application development and maintenance.

https://x.com/Infosys/status/2110022600030122416

Asked about the viability of India's IT services industry as AI advances, Parekh said the growth showed there was "a huge demand" for such services, and that his sense was it is good news for Infosys and, by the same view, good news for tech services in India.

Hiring through the shift

Infosys hired 20,000 fresh graduates last year and plans to recruit another 20,000 in the current financial year, Parekh said. The company trains these employees in AI before deploying them to help clients implement the technology and manage organisational change. Of its workforce of around 300,000, approximately 80,000 are already using coding tools on client assignments and some internal projects.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=SmCnrln8MYc

Parekh also pointed to a shift in how enterprise customers buy AI: while demand remains strong, clients are increasingly testing whether cheaper tokens and open-weight models can deliver the required results, rather than relying exclusively on the newest frontier models.

Why it matters beyond Infosys

Infosys is the bellwether for an Indian IT sector that investors spent much of this year marking down on fears that AI would automate its core work. Parekh's numbers support the opposite read now circulating in markets — that AI deployment itself is becoming the sector's largest growth line. That shift is already visible in share prices: Infosys stock has rallied about 8% over five sessions, part of the broader "anti-AI trade" we report in Indian IT Shares Surge as 'Anti-AI' Trade Lifts Nifty IT. The number to watch in coming quarters is whether total revenue growth accelerates with the AI share, or whether AI work mainly replaces existing contracts.
